Market insiders report that the average cathode import premium over the past fortnight rose slightly to $73/t. The market has been responding to a huge oversupply since March, but business conditions now appear to have stabilised and the active price range has narrowed, with most premiums agreed between $65/t and $80/t. SXEW cathode premiums have been flat from late May at US$50-70/t. After a 150,000t decline in stock levels at Shanghai bonded warehouses from mid-May to early-June, bonded stocks rose slightly over the last two weeks, up by 50,000t to reach 550,000t. Customs data indicates that © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** **June 2012** www.crugroup.com exports of cathode from China recorded a record high level in May, reaching 102,375t up from only 27,420t in April. Reports suggest that it was this prolific cathode export activity that was the reason for the decline in bonded stocks. However, market participants over the past month have suggested that June exports will not reach such levels again. Exports for this month are still expected to be high in comparison to historical levels, as export trade continued from the previous month into the first working week of June. As described in the previous issue, we attribute most of the exports to Chinese smelters covering short positions on the LME, following the differential between cash and 3-month copper contracts flipping into backwardation from March through to May. Despite the negative SHFE/LME arbitrage, cathode imports in May registered 301,990t. Compared to 2011, this was 102.6% higher, bringing the year-to-date increase to 80.2%. We expect China’s refined imports in June to remain at a similar level to May due to the combined effects of a pick-up in demand and a fall in cathode exports. # Uncharacteristic trade There are several likely causes of the record-setting exports of cathode in May. In our 11th May issue, we described how legislation has been changed to grant smelters the opportunity to allow more tolling, i.e. the processing of copper concentrates strictly for the purpose of exporting cathode. This could well account for some of the growth seen in exports, as weak demand in China and low LME warehouse st

ocks caused a favourable arbitrage for these smelters to sell to the LME market. However, a more immediate cause is, as already mentioned, some Chinese smelters exposure to the backwardation on the LME. In order to counteract the backwardation, they shipped sufficient metal to LME warehouses in the region. LME warehouse stocks rose by over 35,000t in May and have risen again by over 35,000t so far in June. The rate of increase has slowed over the last few days, as the lag in shipping times means that the Chinese exports in the early part of June are only just being placed in LME warehouses. On the other side of the trade equation, compared to April Chinese cathode imports rose by 29,087t m-o-m to 301,990t. However, after measuring that against a month of record exports, China’s net refined imports actually fell by 45,868t m-o-m to reach 199,615t in May. Net stock levels (SHFE and bonded) in China fewll month-end to month-end in May by around 32,000t. With domestic refined production registering approximately flat growth, we estimate that cathode demand fell by almost 50,000t m-o-m last month. Part of the reason for the rise in imports was due to a huge increase in imports from the USA. The latest data revealed that China received 30,572t of exports from the US in May, which represents an all-time-high. LME cancelled warrants in the USA continued to fall in May and after considering freight time lags it seems that China will likely continue to receive large volumes of metal from the US in June. These US exports are difficult to explain in terms of the market economics that prevailed in April and May. The large LME/SHFE arbitrage made it relatively unprofitable to ship metal into China, unless it was due to a supplier needing to source metal to meet contractual commitments that it could not do from its usual source of supply. © 2012 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 4 **June 2012** www.crugroup.com # Copper prices supported at RMB55,000/t SHFE 3-month price SHFE inventory descent halted

The LME copper price again fell to below US$7,300/t on 22nd June. Over the past two weeks, the cash-to-3 month spread moved into a $10/t contango, following the delivery of metal into LME warehouses as noted above in this fortnightly’s focus piece. The LME price had bounced to over $7,600/t on 19th June. This was a result of improved investor sentiment following the relatively positive outcome of the Greek elections and that central bank’s may engage in further quantitative easing. In China, the backwardation between the physical

market price and SHFE cash-month price has narrowed to an average of RMB200/t since the last report and the backwardation between the SHFE cash-month and 3-month prices also narrowed to around RMB460/t.  Physical market demand appears to be picking up as fabricators report higher order volumes.  In addition, the arbitrage window narrowing supports the conclusion that physical availability in China is tightening, although given the swollen inventory volumes in bonded warehouses it is not tight yet.  The cathode inventory in SHFE warehouses fell further in the week ending 15<sup>th</sup> June to 130,143t, its lowest level since 13<sup>th</sup> January this year.  However, this was down by only 2,278t on the previous week and was followed by inventory rising in the week ending 22<sup>nd</sup> June by 6,941t back to 137,084t.  Prices held at the top end of our range over the past two weeks.  With demand picking up in China we expect that the copper price on SHFE will trade in a RMB52,000-57,000/t range over the remainder of June.
